extracted.intended_audience: educated British public / political readers concerned with the French Revolution and public reform
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century conservative political pamphlet (Burke's Reflections) arguing for preservation of institutions, respect for property and prescription, cautious reform of clergy and nobility, and against violent or wholesale revolutionary measures. The text offers normative claims about what counts as just government, proper use of history, and acceptable reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility's moral and social qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The nobility ought to possess 'virtue, honor, courage, patriotism, and loyalty' and be 'well bred; very officious, humane, and hospitable; in their conversation frank and open; with a good military tone; and reasonably tinctured with literature.' Their conduct toward inferior classes should be good-natured and familiar rather than oppressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke reports his observation that, under the old government, nobles rarely struck even the most abject, ill-treatment of the humble was rare, and abuses in tenancy or partnership were not systematically oppressive. Anti-patterns: habitual dissoluteness, licentious philosophy, and affectations (foolish imitation) that impair natural character. He allows there may be exceptions but treats them as exceptions only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid collective punishment of corporate bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust to punish persons now for the crimes of their ancestors or of a corporate succession: 'Corporate bodies are immortal for the good of the members, but not for their punishment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that using historical crimes as a pedigree to punish present individuals is 'a sort of refinement in injustice.' Example/anti-pattern: the National Assembly's punishment of clergy and nobles broadly because of past abuses; this is condemned as unjust and vengeful rather than corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of history — instruct, don't pervert
rubrics_metrics.description: History should 'draw the materials of future wisdom from the past errors and infirmities of mankind' and not be perverted to 'furnish offensive and defensive weapons for parties in Church and State.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns against attending only to 'shell and husk' of history, which enables people to wage war on fashions rather than causes; history misused becomes a means to revive animosities and authorize new vices. Remedy: use history to identify causes of evils and address those causes, not merely to demolish names or symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address causes of evil, not merely names or offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform should be applied 'to vices, not to names,--to the causes of evil, which are permanent, not to the occasional organs by which they act.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke counsels against resolving to abolish kings, ministers, priests, or councils as names; instead apply remedies to the underlying vices (pride, ambition, avarice, etc.). Anti-pattern: focusing on fashions or symbolic demolitions while the spirit of wickedness transmigrates into new organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: True toleration vs contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: True toleration respects the value of religious doctrines and protects religions; 'those persons who tolerate all opinions, who think none to be of estimation, is a matter of small merit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke distinguishes tolerant people who 'favor, therefore, and they tolerate' because they respect justice and the common ground of religion, from a false toleration that springs from contempt (equal neglect). Anti-pattern: toleration born of disdain or indifference rather than respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of clergy — tempered judgment and defense of decent clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: While abuses and vices exist among clergy, one should not assume 'the body of your clergy had passed those limits of a just allowance.' Many clergy are 'persons of moderate minds and decorous manners' and of learning; vicious individuals are to be distinguished from the order as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke urges inquiry and caution: accusations often stem from those who will profit by punishment. Praise and support are due where clergy have improved; reforms should avoid degrading or plundering the whole order. Anti-pattern: wholesale confiscation and punishment of all prelates which 'favors the vicious' by indiscriminate treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not plunder or confiscate ecclesiastical property indiscriminately
rubrics_metrics.description: The confiscation of church property and degradation of clergy is condemned as unjust and politically dangerous; 'it is in the principle of injustice that the danger lies, and not in the description of persons on whom it is first exercised.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke cites the sale of monastic lands and seizure of bishops' estates as precedents that threaten wider property rights. Anti-pattern: using exaggerated accounts of clerical vice to justify plunder; consequences include destruction of learned clergy and decline of clerical science and erudition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve prescription and property rights as part of natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescription (long-established legal possession) is 'a part of the law of Nature' and the security of property depends on respect for prescription; legislative assemblies that repudiate prescription risk making all property insecure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that the Assembly's claim that its acts need not conform to prescription leads to destruction of property and substitution of arbitrary currency (paper symbols). Example: confiscations beginning with bishops and monasteries but not ending there. Anti-pattern: legislative despotism that overrules established property and forces a new, unstable circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid electioneering methods for clerical appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Making clergy elective and subject to popular election will 'drive out of the clerical profession all men of sobriety' and place church offices into the hands of 'licentious, bold, crafty, factious, flattering wretches' who seek low pensions through intrigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that elective appointment (without qualifications for doctrine or morals) removes safeguards of competence and leads to an erosion of independent, learned clergy. Anti-pattern: replacing patronage (however imperfect) with uninformed or corrupt popular election for spiritual offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of partisan denunciations used to justify seizure
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges of widespread vice are often amplified by those who 'look for profit in their punishment'; enemies make bad witnesses and robbers worse. Therefore condemnations should be treated with suspicion when they serve as pretext for plunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes that calumnies are ransacked from histories of former ages to justify contemporary confiscations; policy-makers should verify charges and avoid using exaggerated historical examples as a rationale for persecuting contemporary groups.
